terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run the setup to build the repository, then work inside repo/ with git.

tasks.title: Keep a safety net
tasks.description:
Run `node setup.mjs`, then work inside `repo/`.

Before you rewrite anything, create a branch named `route-planner-backup`.

The check expects `route-planner-backup` to point at exactly the last of the five original commits on `route-planner` (`fix typo again`).
nextSteps: Create the backup branch while route-planner still has its original commits.
hints: A branch is just a name for a commit, so a backup costs nothing.
`git branch <name>` with no other argument creates the branch at the commit you are on.
Run it while you are on route-planner and before any reset or rebase. If you already rewrote, look up the old commit in the reflog.

tasks.title: One commit on top of main
tasks.description:
Turn `route-planner` into a single commit.

The check expects:

- `route-planner` is exactly one commit whose parent is `main`'s last commit (`Add fares table`)
- the files on `route-planner` are exactly the same as at the end of the original five commits
- `main` still points at `Add fares table`
- no rebase or merge is left half done, and the working tree is clean

Any non-interactive route works: a soft reset, fixups with autosquash, or a squash merge.
nextSteps: Look at what the branch changes overall with `git diff main route-planner --stat`.
Move route-planner back to main while keeping all its changes staged.
Commit once, then compare the branch with your backup.
hints: You do not need to edit any file. Only the commits change.
One kind of reset moves the branch but leaves the index and files alone.
On route-planner, `git reset --soft main` followed by one `git commit -m` gives one commit. `git diff route-planner-backup route-planner` should then print nothing.

tasks.title: A message worth reading
tasks.description:
Give the squashed commit a clear message.

The check reads the subject (first line) of the last commit on `route-planner` and expects:

- 10 to 72 characters
- no throwaway words such as `wip`, `typo`, `tmp`, `maybe`, `fixup!` or `squash!`
- not one of the original five messages

A body after a blank line is welcome but not required.
nextSteps: Read the diff of the branch and say in one sentence what it adds.
Use that sentence as the subject when you commit.
hints: Write for Ines, who has not seen your scrappy commits.
Start the subject with a verb that describes the change, such as Add or Fix.
If you already committed, `git commit --amend -m "<subject>"` replaces the message of the last commit without an editor.
